stem: A constant force of 20 N pushes a trolley 5 m along the direction of the force. The work done by the force is
explanation: Force and displacement are parallel, so W = Fd = 20 × 5 = 100 J. Dividing 20 by 5 gives 4, which is not a work formula at all, and 200 J doubles the product for no reason.

stem: Ayesha pulls a suitcase with a force of 50 N directed at 60° to the floor and moves it 4 m along the floor. The work done by her pull is
explanation: Only the component along the displacement does work: W = Fd cos θ = 50 × 4 × cos 60° = 200 × ½ = 100 J. Using sin 60° gives 100√3 J, and ignoring the angle gives 200 J.

stem: A stone tied to a string is whirled in a horizontal circle at constant speed. The work done by the tension in the string during one revolution is
options: zero, as force is perpendicular to motion
positive, as the force points to the centre
negative, as the direction keeps changing
explanation: The tension points towards the centre while the displacement at every instant is along the tangent, so θ = 90° and F·d cos 90° = 0 throughout. The speed and kinetic energy stay constant, which confirms that no work is done. Multiplying mv²/r by 2πr wrongly assumes force and displacement are parallel.

stem: One watt is equal to
explanation: Power is the rate of doing work, P = W/t, so 1 W = 1 joule per second = 1 J s⁻¹. The N s and kg m s⁻¹ are units of impulse and momentum, and J s is the unit of Planck's constant, not of power.

stem: The kinetic energy of a 4 kg ball moving at 3 m/s is
explanation: K = ½mv² = ½ × 4 × 3² = ½ × 4 × 9 = 18 J. The value 12 is the momentum mv in kg m/s, and 6 J comes from ½mv, which forgets to square the speed.

stem: If the momentum of a body increases by 50 %, its kinetic energy increases by
explanation: K = p²/2m, so K is proportional to p². The new momentum is 1.5p, so the new K is 1.5² = 2.25 times the old value, an increase of 125 %. The figure 225 % is the new energy as a percentage of the old, not the increase.

stem: Bilal lifts a 2 kg book from a table top 0.8 m above the floor to a shelf 2.3 m above the floor. Taking g = 10 m/s², the gain in gravitational potential energy of the book is
explanation: Only the change in height matters: Δh = 2.3 − 0.8 = 1.5 m, so ΔU = mgΔh = 2 × 10 × 1.5 = 30 J. Using the shelf height alone gives 46 J, and adding the two heights gives 62 J.

stem: A 10 kg crate is pulled 6 m across a level floor at constant velocity. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.3. Taking g = 10 m/s², the work done against friction is
explanation: Friction f = μmg = 0.3 × 10 × 10 = 30 N, and the work against it is f × d = 30 × 6 = 180 J. The value 600 J is mgd, which ignores μ, and 30 is the friction force in newtons, not the work.

stem: A 2 kg ball is thrown vertically upwards and rises 5 m. Taking g = 10 m/s², the work done by gravity on the ball during the rise is
explanation: Gravity (20 N) acts downwards while the ball moves 5 m upwards, so θ = 180° and W = 20 × 5 × cos 180° = −100 J. The value +100 J is the work done against gravity, which equals the gain in potential energy, not the work done by gravity.

stem: Usman holds a 20 kg bag at a fixed height and walks 10 m along a level corridor at constant speed. Taking g = 10 m/s², the work done by his upward supporting force on the bag is
explanation: The supporting force is vertical while the displacement is horizontal, so W = Fd cos 90° = 0. The value 2000 J multiplies the weight (200 N) by the horizontal distance, which treats perpendicular vectors as parallel.

stem: The force on a body increases uniformly from 0 to 40 N as the body moves from x = 0 to x = 0.5 m along the direction of the force. The work done by the force is
explanation: For a variable force, work is the area under the force-displacement graph. Here it is a triangle: ½ × 0.5 × 40 = 10 J. Taking the full rectangle 40 × 0.5 = 20 J forgets that the force was smaller at the start.

stem: A spring of spring constant 200 N/m is stretched by 10 cm from its natural length. The work done in stretching it is
explanation: W = ½kx² = ½ × 200 × (0.1)² = 100 × 0.01 = 1 J. Forgetting the ½ gives 2 J, and 20 is the final force kx in newtons rather than the work.

stem: A spring with k = 500 N/m is already stretched by 2 cm. The extra work needed to stretch it further, from 2 cm to 4 cm, is
explanation: W = ½k(x₂² − x₁²) = ½ × 500 × (0.04² − 0.02²) = 250 × (0.0016 − 0.0004) = 250 × 0.0012 = 0.3 J. The value 0.1 J is ½k(0.02)², which treats the extra 2 cm as if it started from the natural length; the restoring force is already larger there, so more work is needed.

stem: A crane lifts a 500 kg load vertically through 12 m in 20 s at steady speed. Taking g = 10 m/s², the power developed by the crane is
explanation: Work done = mgh = 500 × 10 × 12 = 60 000 J, and P = W/t = 60 000/20 = 3000 W = 3 kW. The figure 60 kW forgets to divide by the time, and 0.3 kW leaves out g.

stem: A car engine provides a forward driving force of 2000 N while the car moves at a steady 25 m/s. The power delivered by the engine is
explanation: P = W/t = F × (d/t) = Fv = 2000 × 25 = 50 000 W = 50 kW. Dividing force by speed gives 80 W (0.08 kW), which has no physical meaning here; 5 kW and 500 kW are power-of-ten slips.

stem: A car whose engine has a maximum power of 60 kW reaches a top speed of 30 m/s on a level road. At top speed, the total resistive force on the car is
explanation: At top speed the driving force equals the resistance, and P = Fv gives F = P/v = 60 000/30 = 2000 N. Using 60 instead of 60 000 W gives 2 N, and multiplying P by v gives 1.8 × 10⁶, which is not a force.

stem: A pump raises 300 kg of water every minute from a well 20 m deep and delivers it at the top with a speed of 10 m/s. The pump is 50 % efficient. Taking g = 10 m/s², the input power of the pump is
explanation: Each minute the water gains PE = 300 × 10 × 20 = 60 000 J and KE = ½ × 300 × 10² = 15 000 J, a total of 75 000 J. Useful output power = 75 000/60 = 1250 W, so input = 1250/0.5 = 2500 W = 2.5 kW. Ignoring the kinetic energy gives 2 kW, and 1.25 kW forgets the efficiency.

stem: According to the work-energy principle, the work done by the net force on a body is equal to the change in its
explanation: The work-energy principle states W(net) = ½mv₂² − ½mv₁² = ΔK. The work done against gravity alone equals the change in potential energy, but the net force (all forces together) changes the kinetic energy. Momentum changes by the impulse, not by the work.

stem: A 20 g bullet moving at 400 m/s enters a wooden block and stops after penetrating 10 cm. The average resistive force exerted by the wood is
explanation: By the work-energy principle F × d = ½mv² = ½ × 0.02 × 400² = 1600 J, so F = 1600/0.1 = 16 000 N. The value 1600 is the kinetic energy in joules, not the force, and 32 000 N forgets the ½.

stem: A 2 kg block starts from rest on a smooth horizontal surface and is acted on by a constant horizontal net force of 8 N over a distance of 4 m. Its final speed is
explanation: Work done = 8 × 4 = 32 J = ½ × 2 × v², so v² = 32 and v = 4√2 m/s. Forgetting the ½ gives mv² = 32 and v = 4 m/s, and 16 m/s is the value of v² after that slip, before taking the square root.

stem: A ball is dropped from rest from a height of 20 m. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m/s², its speed when it is 5 m above the ground is
explanation: It has fallen 20 − 5 = 15 m, so ½mv² = mg × 15 and v = √(2 × 10 × 15) = √300 = 10√3 m/s. Using the height above the ground (5 m) instead of the distance fallen gives 10 m/s, and 20 m/s is the speed on reaching the ground.

stem: A simple pendulum bob is released from rest at a point 45 cm above its lowest position. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m/s², its speed at the lowest point is
explanation: Loss of PE = gain of KE: mgh = ½mv², so v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 10 × 0.45) = √9 = 3 m/s. The value 9 is v² without the square root, and 2.1 m/s comes from √(gh), which drops the factor 2.

stem: A block is released from rest at the top of a smooth curved track 5 m high. At the bottom it moves onto a rough horizontal floor where the coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.25. The distance it slides on the floor before stopping is
explanation: All the PE becomes work against friction on the floor: mgh = μmg d, so d = h/μ = 5/0.25 = 20 m. The mass and g cancel. Multiplying instead of dividing gives μh = 1.25 m.

stem: The escape velocity from the surface of a planet of mass M and radius R is
explanation: For escape the KE must equal the magnitude of the PE at the surface: ½mv² = GMm/R, giving v = √(2GM/R). The expression √(GM/R) is the orbital speed of a satellite just above the surface, which is smaller by a factor √2.

stem: The escape velocity from the Earth is 11.2 km/s. A planet has 8 times the mass of the Earth and twice its radius. The escape velocity from this planet is
explanation: v = √(2GM/R), so v is proportional to √(M/R). Here M/R becomes 8/2 = 4 times larger, so v becomes √4 = 2 times larger: 2 × 11.2 = 22.4 km/s. Forgetting the square root gives 4 × 11.2 = 44.8 km/s.

stem: The escape velocity from the surface of a planet depends on
options: the mass of the escaping body
the angle of launch and the body's mass
the mass and radius of the planet
explanation: From ½mv² = GMm/R the mass m of the body cancels, leaving v = √(2GM/R), which contains only the planet's mass and radius. Energy is a scalar, so the direction of projection does not matter either (ignoring air resistance).

stem: The escape velocity from the Earth is 11.2 km/s. A planet has the same average density as the Earth but half its radius. The escape velocity from this planet is
explanation: With M = ρ(4/3)πR³, v = √(2GM/R) = √(8πGρR²/3), so v is proportional to R√ρ. With the same density and half the radius, v = 11.2/2 = 5.6 km/s. The value 7.9 km/s assumes v ∝ √R, forgetting that the mass also shrinks with R³.

stem: A satellite orbiting just above the surface of a planet moves at 8 km/s. The escape velocity from the surface of that planet is
explanation: Orbital speed near the surface is √(GM/R) and escape velocity is √(2GM/R), so v(escape) = √2 × 8 = 8√2 km/s (about 11.3 km/s). Dividing by √2 instead gives 4√2 km/s, which would be slower than the orbit itself.

stem: Taking g = 10 m/s² at the surface and the Earth's radius as 6.4 × 10⁶ m, the minimum work needed to take a 1 kg body from the Earth's surface to infinity is
explanation: The PE at the surface is −GMm/R, so the work needed is GMm/R. Since GM = gR², this is mgR = 1 × 10 × 6.4 × 10⁶ = 6.4 × 10⁷ J. The value 1.28 × 10⁸ J is 2gR, which is v² for escape, not ½v².

stem: A stone falls freely from a cliff with no air resistance. Which of the following is correct while it falls?
options: Its loss of PE equals its gain of KE
explanation: With gravity as the only force, mechanical energy is conserved: as the stone loses height, every joule of PE lost appears as a joule of KE. The KE grows because the speed increases, and the PE falls because the height decreases.

stem: An electric motor takes 2 kW of electrical power and lifts a 100 kg load through 6 m in 4 s at steady speed. Taking g = 10 m/s², the efficiency of the motor is
explanation: Useful output power = mgh/t = 100 × 10 × 6/4 = 1500 W, so efficiency = 1500/2000 × 100 % = 75 %. Inverting the ratio gives 133 %, which is impossible since no machine gives out more than it takes in; 7.5 % leaves out g.

stem: A 1000 kg car accelerates uniformly from rest to 20 m/s in 10 s on a level road. Ignoring friction, the average power delivered to the car is
explanation: Gain in KE = ½ × 1000 × 20² = 200 000 J, and average power = 200 000/10 = 20 000 W = 20 kW. Forgetting the ½ gives 40 kW; 200 is the energy in kJ, not the power.

stem: A 1000 kg car accelerates uniformly from rest to 20 m/s in 10 s on a level road. Ignoring friction, the instantaneous power delivered at the end of the 10 s is
explanation: a = 20/10 = 2 m/s², so the force is F = ma = 2000 N, and at t = 10 s the power is P = Fv = 2000 × 20 = 40 kW. The value 20 kW is the average power over the 10 s; with constant force the power rises linearly with v, so the final value is twice the average.

stem: Sana, of mass 60 kg, runs up a staircase that rises 4 m vertically over a horizontal distance of 3 m, taking 8 s. Taking g = 10 m/s², her average power against gravity is
explanation: Work against gravity depends only on the vertical rise: mgh = 60 × 10 × 4 = 2400 J, so P = 2400/8 = 300 W. Using the slant length of 5 m gives 375 W, and using the horizontal 3 m gives 225 W.

stem: The kinetic energy K of a body of mass m is related to its linear momentum p by
explanation: K = ½mv² and p = mv, so v = p/m and K = ½m(p/m)² = p²/2m. Writing p²m/2 puts the mass in the numerator, which gives the wrong units (kg³ m² s⁻²).

stem: Two bodies of masses 1 kg and 4 kg have equal kinetic energies. The ratio of their momenta (lighter : heavier) is
explanation: p = √(2mK), so with equal K, p is proportional to √m: p₁/p₂ = √(1/4) = 1/2. The ratio 1 : 4 forgets the square root; the heavier body carries more momentum for the same energy.

stem: Two bodies of masses 2 kg and 8 kg have equal momenta. The ratio of their kinetic energies (lighter : heavier) is
explanation: K = p²/2m, so with equal p, K is inversely proportional to m: K₁/K₂ = 8/2 = 4. The ratio 1 : 4 assumes the heavier body has more energy, which is true for equal speeds, not equal momenta.

stem: A car slows from 20 m/s to 10 m/s. The fraction of its kinetic energy that is lost is
explanation: K is proportional to v², so the new energy is (10/20)² = ¼ of the original, and ¾ = 75 % is lost. Halving the speed does not halve the energy; 50 % treats K as proportional to v.

stem: With a certain constant braking force a car moving at 36 km/h stops in 10 m. With the same braking force, the stopping distance when it moves at 72 km/h is
explanation: Work done by the brakes equals the KE: F d = ½mv², so d is proportional to v². Doubling the speed (10 m/s to 20 m/s) makes the distance 2² = 4 times larger: 40 m. The answer 20 m assumes d is proportional to v.

stem: A 5 kg block starts from rest and slides 4 m down a rough plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. The friction force on it is 10 N. Taking g = 10 m/s², its kinetic energy at the bottom is
explanation: The vertical drop is 4 sin 30° = 2 m, so the PE lost is 5 × 10 × 2 = 100 J. Work against friction is 10 × 4 = 40 J, so KE = 100 − 40 = 60 J. Ignoring friction gives 100 J, and adding the friction work gives 140 J.

stem: A 2 kg block is projected up a rough inclined plane with 50 J of kinetic energy. It comes to rest after rising 2 m vertically. Taking g = 10 m/s², the work done against friction during the ascent is
explanation: The initial KE goes partly into PE and partly into work against friction: 50 = mgh + W(f) = 2 × 10 × 2 + W(f) = 40 + W(f), so W(f) = 10 J. The value 40 J is the gain in PE, not the friction loss.

stem: A small ball rolls without friction from rest down a track that leads into a vertical circular loop of radius r. The minimum starting height above the bottom of the loop for the ball to just complete the loop is
explanation: At the top of the loop the weight alone must supply the centripetal force, so v² = gr there. Energy conservation gives mgh = mg(2r) + ½m(gr), so h = 2r + r/2 = 5r/2. The answer 2r ignores the speed the ball still needs at the top.

stem: A pendulum bob hangs on a light string 1.6 m long. It is pulled aside until the string makes 60° with the vertical and released. Taking g = 10 m/s², its speed at the lowest point is
explanation: The bob rises h = L(1 − cos 60°) = 1.6 × ½ = 0.8 m, so v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 10 × 0.8) = √16 = 4 m/s. Taking h = L = 1.6 m gives 4√2 m/s, which would be the speed for a release from the horizontal position.

stem: A spring of spring constant 800 N/m is compressed by 5 cm and used to launch a 0.1 kg ball along a smooth horizontal surface. The speed of the ball as it leaves the spring is
explanation: Elastic PE = ½kx² = ½ × 800 × 0.05² = 1 J, and this becomes ½mv², so v² = 2 × 1/0.1 = 20 and v = 2√5 m/s (about 4.5 m/s). The value 20 is v², before taking the square root.

stem: The expression U = mgh for gravitational potential energy is valid only when
options: h is small compared with the Earth's radius
h is greater than the Earth's radius
explanation: U = mgh assumes g is constant, which is true only near the surface, where h is much less than R. For large heights g falls off with distance and the general form U = −GMm/r must be used. Motion or rest of the body does not affect PE.

stem: Which of the following is a renewable source of energy?
explanation: Wind is driven by the Sun's uneven heating of the atmosphere and is continuously replenished. Coal and natural gas are fossil fuels formed over millions of years, and uranium is a mined nuclear fuel; all three are used up when consumed.

stem: Geothermal energy is obtained from
options: heat in the hot interior of the Earth
the rise and fall of ocean tides
explanation: Geothermal energy uses heat stored in hot rocks below the Earth's surface, for example by producing steam to drive turbines. Tides give tidal energy, burning waste gives biomass energy, and solar cells give solar electricity.

stem: A solar cell converts
options: light energy directly into electrical energy
explanation: A solar (photovoltaic) cell absorbs light and produces an electric current directly, without heating water or moving parts. Electrical to light is what a bulb does, and chemical to electrical is what a battery does.

stem: A body is dropped from rest from a height H. Ignoring air resistance and taking the ground as zero PE, at what height above the ground is its kinetic energy twice its potential energy?
explanation: At height h, PE = mgh and KE = mg(H − h). Setting H − h = 2h gives h = H/3. The value 2H/3 is where the PE is twice the KE, the reverse of what is asked.

stem: The force on a body is 10 N (in the direction of motion) from x = 0 to x = 2 m, and then decreases uniformly to zero at x = 5 m. The total work done by the force from x = 0 to x = 5 m is
explanation: Work is the area under the force-displacement graph: a rectangle 10 × 2 = 20 J plus a triangle ½ × 3 × 10 = 15 J, total 35 J. Treating the force as 10 N all the way gives 50 J, and 20 J counts only the first part.

stem: A uniform chain of mass m and length L lies on a smooth table with one third of its length hanging vertically over the edge. The work needed to pull the hanging part slowly back onto the table is
explanation: The hanging part has mass m/3 and its centre of mass is L/6 below the table top, so the work is (m/3) × g × (L/6) = mgL/18. Taking the centre of mass at the bottom end (L/3 below) gives mgL/9, which overstates the lift.

stem: A 1200 kg car climbs a straight road that rises 1 m for every 20 m travelled along it, at a steady 15 m/s. The resistive forces total 600 N. Taking g = 10 m/s², the power of the engine is
explanation: Along the slope the engine must balance mg sin θ = 1200 × 10 × (1/20) = 600 N plus the 600 N resistance, a total of 1200 N. Then P = Fv = 1200 × 15 = 18 000 W = 18 kW. Ignoring the slope gives 600 × 15 = 9 kW.

stem: A force F = (3i + 4j) N acts on a particle that undergoes a displacement d = (2i − j) m. The work done by the force is
explanation: W = F·d = (3)(2) + (4)(−1) = 6 − 4 = 2 J. Missing the minus sign gives 6 + 4 = 10 J, and 5 is only the magnitude of the force in newtons.

stem: Work done by a constant force is defined as the
options: scalar product of force and displacement
vector product of force and displacement
product of force and the time it acts
explanation: W = F·d = Fd cos θ, a scalar (dot) product, so work has magnitude but no direction. The product of force and time is impulse, and the vector (cross) product of force and a position vector gives torque.

stem: One kilowatt-hour (kWh) of energy is equal to
explanation: 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. Using 60 instead of 3600 seconds (treating an hour as a minute) gives 6 × 10⁴ J.

stem: A 1.5 kW electric heater is used for 4 hours a day for 30 days. The electrical energy it uses is
explanation: Energy = power × time = 1.5 kW × (4 × 30) h = 1.5 × 120 = 180 kWh. The value 6 kWh is the use for one day only, and 180 000 kWh wrongly converts kW to W while keeping the kWh unit.

stem: Taking 1 horsepower = 746 W, a motor rated at 2 hp has a power of about
explanation: 2 hp = 2 × 746 = 1492 W, about 1.5 kW. Dividing by 2 instead of multiplying gives 373 W, and 2000 W treats 1 hp as 1 kW.

stem: A 5 kW pump that is 80 % efficient fills an overhead tank with 1000 kg of water raised through 20 m. Taking g = 10 m/s², the time taken is
explanation: Useful work = mgh = 1000 × 10 × 20 = 200 000 J and useful power = 0.8 × 5000 = 4000 W, so t = 200 000/4000 = 50 s. Ignoring efficiency gives 40 s, and 32 s multiplies that by 0.8 instead of dividing.

stem: A ball is thrown vertically upwards at 20 m/s. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m/s², the height at which its speed has fallen to half the initial value is
explanation: Energy per kilogram: ½u² − ½v² = gh, so ½(400 − 100) = 10h and h = 15 m. Halving the speed leaves only a quarter of the KE, so three quarters has become PE; 10 m wrongly assumes half the KE has been used up.

stem: A ball is thrown vertically upwards from the ground at 20 m/s. Ignoring air resistance and taking the ground as zero PE, its speed at the point where its kinetic and potential energies are equal is
explanation: Total energy is ½mu². Where KE = PE, KE is half of this, so ½mv² = ½ × ½mu², v = u/√2 = 20/√2 = 10√2 m/s. Taking half the speed (10 m/s) gives only a quarter of the KE, not half.

stem: A 0.5 kg ball is dropped from rest from a height of 20 m and reaches the ground at 18 m/s. Taking g = 10 m/s², the energy lost to air resistance is
explanation: PE lost = 0.5 × 10 × 20 = 100 J and KE gained = ½ × 0.5 × 18² = 81 J, so 100 − 81 = 19 J went into work against air resistance. The value 81 J is the KE at the ground, not the loss.

stem: A raindrop falls through the air at its constant terminal speed. Which of the following is correct?
options: Its KE increases as its PE decreases
Its total mechanical energy is conserved
Its PE stays constant while its KE decreases
Its loss of PE goes into heating the air and the drop
explanation: At terminal speed the KE is constant, yet the drop keeps losing height and PE. That lost PE is used up as work against air resistance and appears as internal energy (heat) of the air and the drop, so mechanical energy is not conserved.

stem: Masses of 3 kg and 2 kg hang at the two ends of a light string passing over a smooth, light pulley. The system is released from rest. Taking g = 10 m/s², the speed of each mass when the 3 kg mass has descended 1 m is
explanation: Net PE lost = (3 − 2) × 10 × 1 = 10 J, shared as KE by both masses moving at the same speed: ½(3 + 2)v² = 10, so v² = 4 and v = 2 m/s. The value 2√5 m/s is √(2gh), which treats the 3 kg mass as falling freely.

stem: A 1 kg block is dropped from rest from a height of 40 cm above the top of a light vertical spring of spring constant 1000 N/m. Taking g = 10 m/s², the maximum compression of the spring is
explanation: At maximum compression x the block is momentarily at rest, so mg(h + x) = ½kx²: 10(0.4 + x) = 500x². Trying x = 0.1 m: 10 × 0.5 = 5 J and 500 × 0.01 = 5 J, so x = 10 cm. About 9 cm comes from ignoring the extra drop x in the PE term, and 1 cm is the equilibrium compression mg/k.

stem: The area under a power-time graph represents
explanation: P = dW/dt, so the area under the P-t graph is the sum of P × Δt, which is the work done (energy transferred). Momentum change is the area under a force-time graph instead.

stem: For a body moving in a straight line, the slope of a graph of its kinetic energy against displacement gives
options: the power delivered to the body
the net force on the body
explanation: By the work-energy principle ΔK = F(net) × Δx, so ΔK/Δx = F(net), the slope of the K-x graph. The slope of K against time, not displacement, would give the power.

stem: Stretching a spring by x from its natural length needs work W. The extra work needed to stretch it further, from x to 2x, is
explanation: Work = ½kx², so stretching to 2x from the natural length needs ½k(2x)² = 4W. The extra work from x to 2x is 4W − W = 3W. The answer 4W is the total from zero, not the extra.

stem: A small planet has surface gravity 1.6 m/s² and radius 1.8 × 10⁶ m. The escape velocity from its surface is
explanation: With GM = gR², v = √(2GM/R) = √(2gR) = √(2 × 1.6 × 1.8 × 10⁶) = √(5.76 × 10⁶) = 2400 m/s = 2.4 km/s. Leaving out the 2 gives √(gR), about 1.7 km/s, which is the orbital speed near the surface.

stem: Ignoring air resistance, a body projected from the Earth's surface with a speed slightly greater than 11.2 km/s will
options: escape from the Earth's gravitational field
orbit the Earth just above its surface
rise very high and then fall back
stop at a finite height and stay there
explanation: 11.2 km/s is the Earth's escape velocity: with this KE the body can overcome the whole gravitational PE GMm/R and never return. A speed of about 7.9 km/s gives a low orbit, and speeds below 11.2 km/s (and not in orbit) make it fall back.

stem: A body is projected from the surface of a planet with a speed twice the escape velocity vₑ. Ignoring air resistance, its speed when it is very far from the planet is
explanation: Energy conservation: ½mv² − GMm/R = ½mv∞², and GMm/R = ½mvₑ². So v∞² = (2vₑ)² − vₑ² = 3vₑ² and v∞ = √3 vₑ. Subtracting speeds directly (2vₑ − vₑ = vₑ) is wrong because energy depends on v².

stem: A body is projected vertically upwards from the surface of a planet of radius R with a speed equal to half the escape velocity. Ignoring air resistance, the maximum height it reaches above the surface is
explanation: With vₑ² = 2GM/R, the initial KE is ½m(vₑ/2)² = GMm/4R. Energy conservation: GMm/4R − GMm/R = −GMm/(R + h), so 3/(4R) = 1/(R + h), R + h = 4R/3 and h = R/3. Using h = v²/2g with constant g gives R/4, which ignores the weakening of gravity with height.

stem: Hamza uses a pulley system to raise an 80 kg load through 1 m. He applies an effort of 250 N and pulls his end of the rope through 4 m. Taking g = 10 m/s², the efficiency of the system is
explanation: Useful output = mgh = 80 × 10 × 1 = 800 J and input = 250 × 4 = 1000 J, so efficiency = 800/1000 = 80 %. Inverting gives 125 %, which is impossible for a real machine.

stem: The efficiency of a real machine is always less than 100 % because
options: some input energy becomes heat and other unwanted forms
energy is destroyed inside the machine
its output work is greater than its input work
a machine cannot change the direction of a force
explanation: Energy is never destroyed, but friction and other losses turn part of the input into heat, sound and other forms that are not useful output. So useful output is always less than input, and efficiency = output/input × 100 % is below 100 %.

stem: A thermal power station burns fuel at a rate that releases 500 MJ of energy every second and delivers 150 MW of electrical power. The energy wasted as heat every second is
explanation: Input power is 500 MW and useful output is 150 MW (efficiency 30 %), so the waste is 500 − 150 = 350 MW, that is 350 MJ each second. Adding the two gives 650 MJ, which counts the output as a loss.

stem: At a small hydroelectric plant, 200 kg of water falls through 50 m every second onto a turbine. The plant converts 80 % of this energy into electrical energy. Taking g = 10 m/s², its electrical power output is
explanation: Power available = (m/t)gh = 200 × 10 × 50 = 100 000 W = 100 kW, and output = 0.8 × 100 = 80 kW. The value 100 kW ignores the efficiency, and 125 kW divides by 0.8 instead of multiplying.

stem: A 2000 kg truck moves on a level road with its engine working at a constant 40 kW. The resistive forces total 1000 N. Its acceleration at the instant its speed is 10 m/s is
explanation: Driving force F = P/v = 40 000/10 = 4000 N, net force = 4000 − 1000 = 3000 N, so a = 3000/2000 = 1.5 m/s². Forgetting the resistance gives 2 m/s².

stem: The work done by gravity on a body that moves along any closed path and returns to its starting point is
explanation: Gravity is a conservative force: the work it does depends only on the start and end heights, W = mg(h₁ − h₂). For a closed path h₁ = h₂, so W = 0. Multiplying mg by the path length would be correct only for friction-like forces, which are non-conservative.

stem: From the top of a tower, Zainab throws one ball vertically upwards and another vertically downwards, both with the same speed. Ignoring air resistance, their speeds on reaching the ground are
options: greater for the one thrown upwards
greater for the one thrown downwards
explanation: Both start with the same KE and the same height, so by energy conservation ½mv² = ½mu² + mgh gives the same v for both. The upward ball takes longer, but when it comes back down past the tower top it again has speed u downwards.

stem: A 2 kg block moving at 4 m/s slides 1 m across a rough floor (coefficient of kinetic friction 0.3) and then onto a smooth section where it hits a light spring of spring constant 500 N/m. Taking g = 10 m/s², the maximum compression of the spring is
explanation: Initial KE = ½ × 2 × 4² = 16 J; work against friction = 0.3 × 2 × 10 × 1 = 6 J, leaving 10 J. Then ½ × 500 × x² = 10 gives x² = 0.04 and x = 0.2 m = 20 cm. Ignoring friction gives x² = 32/500, about 25 cm.

stem: The velocity of a 2 kg body changes from (3i + 4j) m/s to (6i + 8j) m/s. The work done by the net force on the body is
explanation: Speeds are √(9 + 16) = 5 m/s and √(36 + 64) = 10 m/s, so W = ΔK = ½ × 2 × (10² − 5²) = 100 − 25 = 75 J. The value 25 J uses ½m(Δv)² with |Δv| = 5 m/s, which is not the change in kinetic energy, and 100 J is the final KE alone.

stem: A book slides across a rough table and comes to rest. The work done by friction on the book is
explanation: Friction acts opposite to the displacement, so θ = 180° and W = fd cos 180° = −fd. This negative work removes the book's kinetic energy, which is why it stops. It is not zero, because the force is along the line of motion.

stem: A 0.2 kg cricket ball is moving at 30 m/s. Its kinetic energy is
explanation: K = ½mv² = ½ × 0.2 × 30² = 0.1 × 900 = 90 J. The value 6 is the momentum mv in kg m/s, and 3 J comes from ½mv without squaring the speed.

stem: A boy does 1200 J of work in 1 minute. His average power is
explanation: P = W/t = 1200/60 = 20 W, with the time in seconds. Leaving the time as 1 gives 1200 W, and multiplying by 60 gives 72 000 W, which is not a power at all.

stem: A water tank holding 2000 kg of water is placed on a roof 15 m above the ground. Taking g = 10 m/s², the gravitational PE of the water relative to the ground is
explanation: U = mgh = 2000 × 10 × 15 = 300 000 J = 3 × 10⁵ J. Leaving out g gives 3 × 10⁴ J, one power of ten too small.

stem: If the speed of a moving car is doubled, its kinetic energy becomes
explanation: K = ½mv² is proportional to v², so doubling v multiplies K by 2² = 4. Twice as large would be true only if K were proportional to v, as momentum is.

stem: A 10 kg box is lifted vertically through 2 m with a constant upward acceleration of 2 m/s². Taking g = 10 m/s², the work done by the lifting force is
explanation: Lifting force F = m(g + a) = 10 × 12 = 120 N, so W = 120 × 2 = 240 J. Of this, 200 J becomes PE and 40 J becomes KE. The value 200 J would apply only for lifting at constant speed.

stem: A swing passes through its lowest point at 2 m/s. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m/s², the greatest height it rises above the lowest point is
explanation: ½mv² = mgh gives h = v²/2g = 4/20 = 0.2 m = 20 cm. Forgetting the 2 in the denominator gives 40 cm.

stem: Crane A lifts a load to a certain height in 10 s; crane B lifts an identical load to the same height in 20 s. Which statement is correct?
options: A does twice as much work as B
B develops twice the power of A
Both do equal work, but A has twice the power
explanation: Work = mgh is the same for both, since the load and height are the same. Power = W/t, so A, taking half the time, has twice the power. Taking longer does not mean doing more work.

stem: A force of 20 N stretches a spring by 4 cm. The elastic potential energy stored in the spring is
explanation: k = F/x = 20/0.04 = 500 N/m, so U = ½kx² = ½ × 500 × 0.04² = 0.4 J (equivalently ½Fx = ½ × 20 × 0.04). The value 0.8 J is Fx, which treats the force as 20 N from the very start, and 40 J keeps x in centimetres.

stem: The Moon has practically no atmosphere mainly because
options: its low escape velocity lets gas molecules escape
it has no gravitational field at all
it is too cold for any gas to exist
its surface reflects most of the sunlight
explanation: The Moon's escape velocity is only about 2.4 km/s, and fast-moving gas molecules heated by the Sun can reach such speeds and leave. The Moon does have gravity (about one sixth of the Earth's), just not enough to hold an atmosphere.

stem: A 60 W filament lamp gives out light energy at a rate of 6 W. The energy wasted as heat in one minute is
explanation: Wasted power = 60 − 6 = 54 W, and in 60 s the waste is 54 × 60 = 3240 J (the efficiency is only 10 %). The value 3600 J is the total input in a minute, and 54 J is the waste in one second.

stem: A 1500 kg car moving at 20 m/s is brought to rest by its brakes. The work done by the braking force is
explanation: By the work-energy principle, W = 0 − ½mv² = −½ × 1500 × 400 = −3 × 10⁵ J. It is negative because the braking force opposes the motion; forgetting the ½ gives −6 × 10⁵ J.

stem: A 2 kg block slides from rest down a rough plane 10 m long, inclined at 30° to the horizontal, and reaches the bottom at 8 m/s. Taking g = 10 m/s², the average friction force on the block is
explanation: Height = 10 sin 30° = 5 m, so PE lost = 2 × 10 × 5 = 100 J and KE gained = ½ × 2 × 64 = 64 J. Work against friction = 36 J over 10 m, so f = 3.6 N. The value 36 is the friction work in joules, and 6.4 N divides the KE by the length.

stem: A pump draws water from a tank and ejects it through a nozzle 5 m higher at 10 m/s, at a rate of 2 kg every second. Taking g = 10 m/s² and ignoring losses, the power of the pump is
explanation: Each second the water gains PE = 2 × 10 × 5 = 100 J and KE = ½ × 2 × 10² = 100 J, so P = 200 W. Using mv² instead of ½mv² for the KE gives 300 W, and 100 W counts only one of the two energies.

stem: The escape velocity from the Earth is 11.2 km/s. A planet has twice the Earth's surface gravity and half its radius. The escape velocity from this planet is
explanation: v = √(2gR), so v is proportional to √(gR). Here gR becomes 2 × ½ = 1 times the Earth's value, so the escape velocity is unchanged at 11.2 km/s. Taking only the change in g gives √2 × 11.2 ≈ 15.8 km/s.
